newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Petrol bomber Mohammad taunts Israeli soldiers.
newsitem.headline: Petrol bomber Mohammad taunts Israeli soldiers.

text.p: Petrol bomb in hand, Mohammad taunted Israeli soldiers just a few metres away to come and get him.
Mohammad threw the flaming bottle. Israeli snipers took aim at the teenager in the Hebron alleyway and fired. A 10-year-old boy next to him was hit in the leg.

"Look at you, all armed to the teeth and protected. I challenge you to throw down your guns and come to me," Mohammad shouted in Hebrew. "You're cowards, if you come to me without your guns I will stamp on you like cockroaches."

Mohammad was one of dozens of youths who took to the streets in the divided West Bank city on Wednesday in a wave of anger touched off by the pasting on storefronts of posters depicting the Moslem Prophet Mohammad as a pig stamping on the holy Koran.
A 25-year-old Jewish woman from Jerusalem was under arrest on suspicion of gluing the posters.
Israeli soldiers, pelted by rocks and petrol bombs, wounded 37 Palestinians on Wednesday in Hebron.
Youths whislted and cheered as boys set fire to an Israeli flag. Arab residents of Hebron observed a general strike called to protest against the anti-Moslem posters discovered on Saturday.
Israeli soldiers deployed across rooftops and alleyways and inside Palestinians homes along the dividing line between Israeli and PLO-controlled sectors of Hebron to confront the protesters.
The posters, desecrating the name of the prophet and Islam's holy book, were something traditionally religious, conservative Hebronites could not tolerate.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's public apology to Moslems was not sufficient for the Palestinians of Hebron.

"The settlers and the soldiers who protect them have to pay the price for the provocative posters," said one of the leaders of the "shabab", Arabic for youth, as he prepared a petrol bomb. "There will be no peace or calm in the city as long as the settlers live in Hebron."
Protests were organised by small groups of youths operating from a deserted house behind the confrontation lines in Hebron.
Youths ran a makeshift assembly line which funneled petrol stored in a large bin into empty cola bottles and topped them off with a bit of cloth.
Teenagers lit the homemade Molotov cocktails and ferried them to the frontlines to be hurled at Israeli troops.
Other youngsters in the dusty house pulled out floor tiles, while boys filled buckets with the stones and carried the fresh ammunition to protesters in the alleyways.
Palestinian police stayed a few meters away from the frontline and directed traffic as if the street battles did not exist.
"We did not go to the friction areas because the youths would have used us as a shield, drawing fire in our direction and causing escalation of unrest," one policeman said.

Israel handed over 80 percent of Hebron to PLO rule in January but troops stayed on to guard 400 Jews who had settled in fortified enclaves in the heart of the city revered by Moslems and Jews as the burial place of the biblical Abraham.

PLO officials said the unrest was also a reflection of growing Palestinian frustration over deadlocked peace moves which came to a halt in March after Israel began building a new settlement on occupied land in Jerusalem.
